To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we established a novel method to identify the sequences flanking screening elements in genetically modified organisms (GM) and we developed a collection of in-silico calculated fingerprints of GM events to support identification of unknown GM events.

(1) anchor PCR allows the identification of the unique sequences flanking the screening elements p35S and nos, (2) in silico calculated anchor-PCR fingerprints of known events allow the interpretation of experimentally obtained anchor-PCR fingerprints and the identification of unknown events, and (3) the new molecular toolbox allows the molecular identification of an unknown GMO.
the new methods allow the identification of unknown events without the need to sequence the event-specific DNA.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of new molecular tools to improve GMO detection and identification.
the improvement of analytical detection of GMOs in general and of unknown events in particular.
the development of new methods to support the identification of unknown GMOs.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the novel GMO is a new event that has not yet been registered and is therefore unknown.
a GMO event is not identified in a sample if the screening elements p35S and/or t-nos are not detected and if all known events are tested but are not detected.
an unknown event was detected and characterized in a blind sample.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have developed a toolbox of molecular methods to identify unknown genetically modified organisms (unknown GMOs) and to support the detection of unauthorized GMOs in food and feed.
we developed a toolbox for the identification, detection and characterization of GMOs, which can be used for the analysis of GMOs and products derived thereof.
we have established a molecular toolbox for the identification and characterization of unknown GMOs and have demonstrated its applicability in a real-life situation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the molecular toolbox presented here can be applied to any event-specific detection method and can therefore be used to identify any unknown event.

the combination of the new methods with existing routine procedures may lead to a more robust identification of novel GMOs and may also be helpful to resolve the masking of unknown events in samples with multiple known events.
anchor-PCR fingerprint analysis and in silico event fingerprinting provide an additional molecular toolbox for the detection of unknown events.
